extracted.intended_audience: media/cultural studies students and scholars; communication researchers; media practitioners interested in theory of encoding/decoding
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and analytical framework for understanding how television (and similar media) messages are produced, encoded, circulated, and decoded by audiences, including the institutional, technical and ideological conditions that shape meaning and reading positions. Emphasizes the non-equivalence of encoding and decoding and the plural modes of audience interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moments of the communicative process (production–circulation–consumption–reproduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptualize communication as a structure produced through linked but distinctive moments: production, circulation, distribution/consumption, reproduction, each with its specific modality and conditions of existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these moments as articulated parts of a complex structure in dominance: each moment is necessary to the circuit as a whole but can interrupt or break the flow; analysis should consider how each moment shapes the 'forms' of the message and their continuity across the circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message form / Discursive form as a determinate moment
rubrics_metrics.description: The discursive or 'message form' is a necessary, determinate moment in the communicative process: events must be signified (become a 'story') and pass under the rules of language before they can circulate as messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat transposition into/out of the message form as random or optional; evaluate how formal sub-rules of discourse operate 'in dominance' when constituting the televisual message and shaping what can be communicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material instruments and social relations of production
rubrics_metrics.description: Production requires material instruments ('means') and sets of social production relations—the organization and combination of practices within media apparatuses—which frame the constitution of programmes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for technical infrastructures, routines of production, historically defined skills, professional ideologies and institutional knowledge when assessing how messages are encoded; production structures both originate discourse and draw from wider socio-cultural formations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of decoded meanings into social practices (realization/use)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the communicative circuit to be completed and effective, decoded meanings must be translated into social practices; if meaning is not taken or articulated in practice it has no effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess not only the signification of messages but whether and how audiences appropriate meanings into practice (use, influence, persuasion, behavioral or ideological consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Encoding–decoding non-correspondence and degrees of symmetry/asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no necessary or automatic correspondence between the codes of encoding and the codes of decoding; degrees of identity or non-identity (symmetry/asymmetry) between meaning-structures determine how messages are transmitted, interrupted, or distorted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate communicative exchanges in terms of code fit or mismatch; examine structural differences in relation and position between producers and audiences that produce distortions or misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: No degree-zero: visual/iconic signs are coded
rubrics_metrics.description: Iconic and visual signs (e.g., televisual images) are coded signs too; there is no 'degree zero' in language—apparent naturalism or fidelity is the result of specific codings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming visual 'naturalness' or transparency; analyze the perceptual 'conditions of perception' and the coding operations that make visual signs seem natural or referential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denotative vs connotative levels of the sign
rubrics_metrics.description: The denotative level of a televisual sign is fixed by complex but bounded codes; the connotative level is more open, subject to active transformations and polysemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating messages, distinguish between relatively constrained denotation and more contestable connotation; trace how connotative configurations are produced by sub-codes and contextual positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polysemy is not pluralism; inequality among connotative codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a sign may be polysemic (open to multiple connotations), connotative codes are not equal — societies impose structured, hierarchical mappings of meanings (dominant cultural orders) that privilege certain readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate multiple possible readings with equal legitimacy; identify the dominant or preferred mappings and how they are institutionally and ideologically supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant cultural order and preferred readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Discursive domains are hierarchically organized into dominant or preferred meanings that carry institutional/political/ideological weight and appear 'natural' or 'taken-for-granted'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how messages are situated within broader 'maps of social reality' and how these dominant orders shape likely decodings; identify the institutional imprints on preferred readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: The labor/work of enforcing a preferred reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a preferred or dominant reading requires interpretative 'work'—performative rules, logics-in-use, competencies and practices that actively enforce or promote one semantic domain over others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the practical mechanisms (presentational choices, formats, staging, selection of personnel, professional routines) used to win plausibility and legitimise a particular decoding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misunderstandings as systematically distorted communication
rubrics_metrics.description: When audiences 'fail' to take the intended meaning, this is often not mere random selective perception but a systematic distortion arising from operating with different codes; broadcasters' goal of transparent communication overlooks this structured non-equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique accounts that reduce variation to 'selective perception'; instead investigate structural and code-based sources of divergent readings and how audience clusters of meanings form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant-hegemonic decoding position
rubrics_metrics.description: A decoding position in which the viewer takes the connoted/encoded meaning fully and straight, decoding the message within the reference code in which it was encoded; closest to 'transparent communication'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when audiences reproduce hegemonic interpretations; note how professional codes and institutional access produce and sustain these readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated decoding position
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed decoding that acknowledges hegemonic definitions at a general level but adapts or resists them in particular, situated ways—accepting dominant logic while making local exceptions or reservations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for decodings that accept grand significations but reinterpret or apply them selectively according to local conditions (e.g., workers agreeing with 'national interest' rhetorically but resisting on the shopfloor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppositional decoding position
rubrics_metrics.description: A decoding that understands the preferred meaning but decodes the message within a globally contrary framework—retotalizing the message into an alternative political or ideological view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize active re-framing and resistance where audiences rework or reject dominant meanings and substitute oppositional interpretive frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production–reception feedback and reincorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation and reception are themselves moments of production; audience reception and images of the audience are drawn back into production via skewed, structured feedbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how audience practices and receptions feed back into production choices, agendas and professional routines; consumption is part of the larger production process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalized codes conceal constructedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes that are broadly distributed and learned early may appear 'natural' or transparent, but this naturalness is the effect of deep habituation and ideological concealment of coding practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to seemingly 'obvious' or 'universal' meanings: interrogate their historical and cultural construction and the ideological effects of their naturalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encoding sets limits but does not determine decoding
rubrics_metrics.description: Encoding constructs limits and parameters that shape possible decodings, but it cannot prescribe or guarantee which decoding codes will be employed; some degree of reciprocity is constructed rather than natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation or production, recognize that while encoding choices matter in delimiting interpretations, audiences retain agency to negotiate, accept, or oppose meanings within those limits.
